title: Everything Else
intro: Frequently asked questions and a few other parts of the club website.
faqTrialHeading: How do I try paddling with the club?
faqTrialAnswer: Open-night sessions run seasonally and need to be booked online. You do not need to be a member to attend, and your first three trial sessions are free. Check the [Beginners page](/beginners) for current details and booking information.
faqMembershipHeading: When do I need to become a member?
faqMembershipAnswer: Membership is required after your first three trial sessions. Current membership options and prices are listed on the [Membership and Events page](/membership); prices can change, so check the live listing.
faqWhatToBringHeading: What should I bring to a session?
faqWhatToBringAnswer: Bring a towel, clothes that can get wet, a warm change of clothes, and flat shoes that will stay on in the water. A wetsuit is optional. See the [Beginners page](/beginners) for current guidance.
faqChildrenAnswer: Young people under 16 must be supervised by an accompanying adult at club nights. Children under 8 may paddle in an open canoe with a supervising adult; children need to be at least 8 to join a kids class or paddle in a one-person boat. Check the [Beginners page](/beginners) before booking.
faqHireHeading: Can I hire a boat or equipment?
faqHireAnswer: Current boat and kit hire options, prices and terms are shown on the [Membership and Events page](/membership). If you need equipment for a single visit or are not yet a member, contact the club before booking to confirm what is available and who can use it.
faqTripsHeading: How do I find out about paddling trips?
faqTripsAnswer: White water trips are organised by request. See the [Disciplines page](/disciplines) for more information, check the [Membership and Events page](/membership) for current listings, or contact the club to ask about a trip.
faqExperiencedHeading: I have paddling experience. How do I join a session?
faqExperiencedAnswer: Contact the club through the [Contact Us page](/contact-us) and describe your experience, qualifications and the discipline you are interested in. A club lead can advise which session is appropriate and whether an introduction or skills check is needed.
faqSupportedHeading: Can the club support paddlers with additional access needs?
faqSupportedAnswer: Please contact our [Supported Paddling coordinator](mailto:supported.paddling@forthcanoeclub.co.uk) before visiting to discuss your needs and confirm current access arrangements. You can also read about the [Access Project](/access-project).
faqClubNightAnswer: On club nights the boathouse is open for members to use club boats; the [weekly timetable](/disciplines) shows the current days and times. A volunteer is on duty in or around the boathouse. They are not necessarily a coach, so club nights are for members who can get themselves safely on and off the water, though they will help if they can. Before you paddle out of sight of the boathouse we need to know you can cope with a capsize in the craft you use: you might be asked to show this, unless you have done it on a course with us or have previous experience. Kit hire charges apply on club nights.
faqCoursesHeading: How do courses for adults work?
faqCoursesAnswer: We run courses in canoeing, kayaking and paddleboarding, including Discover (for beginners) and Explore (for people who have done some paddling before) in canoeing and kayaking. Other courses can be arranged depending on demand and coach availability: if there is something you want to learn that we are not offering, let us know, as we only need three or four people to make a course viable. Kit hire is included in courses. Current courses are on the [Membership and Events page](/membership).
faqPoloAnswer: Polo sessions are on the [weekly timetable](/disciplines). You need to be 14 or over and able to get out of the boat if you capsize. Members are welcome to come along and try it a few times before deciding whether to sign up.
faqSlalomHeading: How do slalom and sprint work?
faqSlalomAnswer: Slalom and sprint sessions are for paddlers aged 14 and over, and are a great way to take your paddling further. See the [Disciplines page](/disciplines) for details.
faqAccessHeading: The boathouse is downstairs. How can a wheelchair user get to the water?
faqAccessAnswer: We are working to make the site more accessible through the [Access Project](/access-project). For now, wheelchair users can come down the ramp in the park to the canal side, where we use Canadian canoes and specialist equipment to transfer paddlers, with all their equipment, across the canal to the clubhouse. Please contact our [Supported Paddling coordinator](mailto:supported.paddling@forthcanoeclub.co.uk) before your visit.
faqVolunteeringAnswer: The club runs on volunteer power and more volunteers are always welcome, from work days getting the boathouse in order to joining the committee. Opportunities are shared in club emails, on the club Facebook page and on the boathouse noticeboard, but if you are keen to get involved just let us know. Volunteers get benefits such as reduced costs, with more for more pledged volunteer hours. See the [Volunteering page](/volunteering) for current roles and benefits.
faqSocialsHeading: What social events and meetings are there?
faqSocialsAnswer: The first and last club nights of the season are usually club barbecues: vegetarian food and soft drinks are free for members, you are welcome to bring your own, and children are welcome. Committee meetings and the AGM are open to all members. At the AGM we get through the formalities quickly, give out awards for the year’s achievements and then socialise. There are occasional other socials too.
historyBody:
Forth Canoe Club has a rich history in the city going back to 1934. Explore our history and how it shaped the club.

1952 | The early pioneer era
Allan Sharples and early Forth Canoe Club members begin recording Scottish canoeing history. Colour film and photography in the early 1950s were expensive commitments, so these records are rare early archives of British kayaking. See the [Allan Sharples photo collection](https://www.canoeingphotos.com/Photo-Collections/Allan-Sharples-Collection).

1955 | Folding craft and tidal rapids
Folding boats (“F1”) are the standard slalom class. Club members, including Allan Sharples, John Roberts, Brian Palmer, Dougal Lauder, Robin Anderson, Neville Eilbeck and David Anderson, pioneer tidal rapid runs down the [Falls of Lora](https://www.fallsoflora.info) and [Corryvreckan](https://isleofjura.scot/paddleboarding-jura-safety-guide-for-the-sound-of-jura-corryvreckan/) in 4-metre folding craft.

1960 | National competition and home-made gear
Cine film captures Marsh Lock (1959) and the British Nationals at Llangollen (1960): see [Allan Sharples’ films](https://www.canoeingphotos.com/Videos/Allan-Sharples-Films). Competitors take racing seriously in full vests, but instead of official BS3595 life jackets they make buoyancy aids by sewing two Dunlopillo camping pillows together with cotton tape.

1963 | The GRP revolution and Thistlebrig
In 1962–1963 GRP (glass reinforced plastic) boats come into slalom. Allan moves to composite hulls costing around £25–£35 (the licensed Isère at £35, or Chris Hawkesworth’s Inn Spezial replica at £27), compared with £75 for a folding Klepper. The club hosts ranking events at Thistlebrig, rigging Sunday “mini-slaloms” with 3mm terylene cord, and cine footage records events at Serpent’s Tail (1962), [Grandtully](https://www.canoeslalom.co.uk/events/venues/grandtully/) (1962–1964) and Builth Wells (1963).

1965 | Peak archives and iconic designs
Footage records the 1965 River Lune trip and the Fairnilee slaloms, hosted with Edinburgh University Canoe Club. Iconic boats of the period include John Critchley’s JayCee Cobra, and Keith White’s British Team slalom boats (KW 3, KW 7) and wildwater racer (KW 4).

1971 | Preserving the heritage
Decades of club history, classic boat designs and early river runs are preserved. Mike Sharples has digitised 28 cine film clips (1959–1965) and 35mm slide collections, now on canoeingphotos.com: see the [films](https://www.canoeingphotos.com/Videos/Allan-Sharples-Films) and the [slide collection](https://www.canoeingphotos.com/Photo-Collections/Allan-Sharples-Collection).

2004 | The canal drained at Lochrin Basin
In February 2004 the canal was drained, and the club’s old buildings at Lochrin Basin were demolished to make room for offices. Photos from Leamington Lift Bridge (J. Riddell) show how wide the canal used to be.

2013 | By Harrison Park
The club on the canal by Harrison Park, a popular spot especially in the school holidays: photos on Blipfoto by [hcalibrarian](https://www.blipfoto.com/entry/3273949) and [onedayandcanal](https://www.blipfoto.com/entry/2310038343066323702).
magazineBody:
In 1973 Forth Canoe Club was 50 years old, and had produced “The Spraysheet” news and also CANews. The inspiration came from the “Edinburgh Schools Newsletter”, published by Edinburgh Outdoor Pursuits Centre and Boroughmuir High School, who ran weekly Wednesday afternoon canoeing trips for school pupils. So a club newsletter started in April 1973, publishing five editions on foolscap (8 × 13 inch) paper and finishing with April 1974.

On the suggestion of Andy Morton, the newsletter grew into Kayak Magazine, sold to several hundred canoeists in Scotland and produced on the new European A4 paper. The production team was Jack, Betty, Gordon and David Cuthill, supported by many other members of Forth Canoe Club and other Scottish clubs. The first edition was published in July 1974 and the magazine ran until 1983.

These were the days before affordable photocopiers, and of course there were no mobile phones, computers or internet: if you could not get to a competition you had entered, you had to write to the organisers. Betty Cuthill typed the pages on to Roneo waxed silk stencils, and they were reproduced on the dining room table with an electric Gestetner duplicator. Advertising came in from August 1975.

From January 1976 a larger A3 cover (420 × 279 mm) allowed photos on the cover, funded by more advertising sponsorship from Lendal Products Ltd (Prestwick), Pyranha Mouldings Ltd (Warrington), Trylon, Tulloch Boat Centre at Canonmills (Edinburgh), Strand Glass, Graham Tiso and Afton Canoes. David Cuthill drew the early covers by scratching the Roneo stencils with a pin; after that he took the photos and developed the black-and-white images. A local printer printed the A3 covers by web-offset lithography.
